newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Steam power hits Rolls-Royce profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Steam power hits Rolls-Royce profits.

text.p: Engineer Rolls-Royce Plc slipped into loss on Thursday, hit by its decision announced last year to withdraw from the market for steam power generation equipment.
But it said operating profits from its core aero-engines and industrial power businesses rose to 242 million pounds ($390 million) in 1996 from 178 million in 1995, boosted by strong order books.
Annual sales excluding businesses to be sold rose to 4.05 billion pounds from 3.34 billion pounds a year ago.

Chairman Sir Ralph Robins said the company delivered around 1,100 aircraft engines last year and expected that this figure would rise in 1997 as output for commercial aircraft was set to be more than the 360 delivered in 1996.

"We will clearly deliver more this year," he told Reuters in an interview. "There is fairly significant growth in the civil business at the moment ... All the aircraft constructors are increasing their build rates and that's finally being reflected on us," he said.

Robins also said the all-important spares market which accounts for around a third of total aerospace business was on the increase, having recovered from the 20 percent fall seen in the early 1990s when airlines had to tighten their belts and cut back on spares inventories.
"As I said at the half-year we are seeing a turnup in spares and that's continued," he said. "We are probably approaching the level now that we were at (before the fall) in 1990."

But Rolls reported an overall pretax loss of 28 million pounds compared with a profit of 175 million pounds in 1995, after booking in 263 million pounds of provisions, write-offs and losses detailed last year for its plan to sell or close its two steam power businesses.
Rolls put the two, Parsons and International Combustion, up for sale in July last year and said it would close the operations if it could not sell them.
But Robins said on Thursday he was now close to selling both.
"There are several bidders for both...and we are confident that we are going to sell both of the businesses and that we will make some announcements in the next few weeks," he told Reuters.
Robins also said the company was making progress in its attempt to sell Canadian subsidiary Bristol Aerospace and hoped for news "probably in the next few weeks".
The Winnipeg-based aircraft maintenance and rocket manufacturer has annual sales of around Canadian $60 million and employs about 1,000 people but was not considered a core business.
"It does a little bit of engine (overhaul) business for us and also for others but it's mainly in the air frame and rocket business," he said.
The final dividend was raised 10 percent to 3.3 pence a share, making 5.3 pence for the year against 5.0 pence last time, on pre-exceptional earnings of 12.7 pence, up from 7.94 pence in 1995.

The share price rose 15 to 254 pence after the news, helped by confirmation that Rolls was giving the first increase in dividend for four years. "They were a good set of results, slightly better than people's expectations," said Paul Pickford, analyst at brokers Panmure Gordon.
